scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The douga originates among the Mandinka people of West Africa as a ceremonial dance and song.
It forms a symbolic chain stretching back to the emperor Sundiata Keita, reflecting the hierarchical, casted order of traditional Mande society.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance marks religious revivals, demonstrates human knowledge and wisdom over bestial instinct, and symbolizes the promise of resurrection of the dead.
It is performed at great ceremonial events.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music features the singing of griots.
It was recorded in 1960 by Mory and Madina Kouyaté, adapted in the 1960s by the Ensemble National de Guinée as 'Armée Guinnéenne,' and later reworked by Bembeya Jazz National as a warrior song.
A traditional vocal delivery by Guinean griots, later adapted into military praise music and Guinean jazz ensemble instrumentation.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ada Uzoamaka Azodo, Christopher Miller, Uzo Esonwanne, Frantz Fanon, Fodéba Keïta, Camara Laye, Jacques Bourgeac, Mory Kouyaté, Madina Kouyaté, Sundiata Keita.
Linked to the ring shouts of the Gullah people on the US Atlantic coast, with resonances in the 19th-century African-American buck dance known as the 'Buzzard lope'.
Rooted in Mandinka and wider Mande traditions, with modern orchestral and jazz adaptations in Guinea.
